# Chapitre 1 · Ouverture: Vue d'ensemble

Tests de performance · Chapitre 1: Vue d'ensemble · 5 min

> Ce que couvre ce cours, comment il est construit et comment utiliser la classe et ses prompts pour agents.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

## Transcription: Overview (1:53)

**0:00 Welcome.** Welcome to Performance Testing on Testbench. In this course you'll learn to find what makes software slow, before your users do. "The site feels slow" is a complaint. A number with a cause attached is a finding. This course teaches you to get from one to the other.

**0:20 Four chapters.** The course has four chapters. First, an overview: what performance testing measures, and how. Then static testing: finding problems by reading code, query plans and build output, without running anything. Then dynamic testing: running the app under realistic traffic and measuring what users feel. And finally a summary that puts both into a workflow, and into a report people can act on.

**0:48 The practice app.** You'll practise on Larkspur Books, a small online bookshop with five thousand books and two hundred thousand orders. It's slow on purpose. One page of books runs a hundred and one database queries, and on a phone the main image takes almost ten seconds to appear. By the end of the course you'll have found and fixed every one of those problems, with a number to prove each fix.

**1:17 How each page works.** Every page works the same way. Watch a short video, like this one. Then read the lesson below it, at your own pace. Then do your part of the hands-on exercise: run the checks yourself, and read the numbers. Hand the implementation to a coding agent. Copy the exercise's prompt, and the agent makes the fix and quotes its output. Then verify: rerun the same check yourself. The number you see is the one that counts, and the decision is yours.

## La leçon

"The site feels slow" is a complaint. "p95 for `/api/books` is 1.3 seconds against a 300 ms budget, because the endpoint runs 101 queries per request" is a finding someone can fix. This course teaches you to get from the first to the second, reliably.

## Ce que vous allez obtenir

- Know what questions performance testing answers, and which numbers it reports
- Tell static testing from dynamic testing, and know when each one pays off
- Have the practice app running, with a first measurement written down
- Know how to hand a hands-on exercise to a coding agent, and what to check when it reports back

## How the course is built

The course moves from the big picture to specific techniques and back again. Chapter 1 frames the problem. Chapters 2 and 3 each go deep on one family of tests. Chapter 4 puts them together into a workflow and a report.

1. **Vue d'ensemble** (Général): Ce que mesure un test de performance, les deux familles de tests et l'application d'entraînement.
2. **Tests statiques** (Spécifique): Trouver les problèmes de performance en examinant ce que vous avez construit, sans l'exécuter.
3. **Tests dynamiques** (Spécifique): Faire tourner le système, lui envoyer du trafic et mesurer ce que ressentent les utilisateurs.
4. **Synthèse** (Général): Réunir les deux dans une routine, rendre compte des résultats, prononcer l'acceptation, l'appliquer à votre propre projet et revoir tout le cours.

Every chapter follows the same shape:

1. **An opening** like this one: what you'll get, and a map of the chapter.
2. **Lessons.** Each mixes concepts and practice. Concepts come with a short **animation** you can play, pause and step through. Hands-on exercises run against the practice app and show **screenshots** of what you should see.
3. **A summary** that collects the chapter's key points and gives you a few questions to check yourself.

## The practice app

Everything you test is **Larkspur Books**, a small bookshop in `academy/practice/larkspur`: a storefront page and three JSON endpoints over a SQLite database of 5,000 books, 50,000 reviews and 200,000 orders. It needs Node.js 22.13 or later and nothing else.

Larkspur is slow on purpose. Each problem in it is one this course teaches you to find, and every number quoted in the lessons comes from a real run against it. Your numbers will differ with your machine; the shape of the results won't.

## Working with an agent

This course teaches you to test performance, and an agent helps you do it. The split is the same in every exercise:

| You | The agent |
| --- | --- |
| Learn the concept: watch, read | |
| Run the checks and tests, read the numbers | |
| | Implement: fixes, scripts, gates, CI configuration |
| | Report back, quoting real command output |
| Verify: rerun the same check and compare | |
| Decide: accept, reject, or set a new budget | |

Each exercise has two parts. **Your part** comes first: the steps you run yourself, with the output you should expect. Then the **agent part**: a prompt you copy into Claude Code or another coding agent, so it makes the changes. The prompt is self-contained: where to work, the steps, how to tell it's done, and what to report. It tells the agent to quote real output instead of estimating, and never to loosen a budget to make a check pass.

When the agent says it's done, rerun the check yourself. The number you see is the one that counts. By the end of the course you'll use the same loop on your own project (lesson 4.4) and finish with a formal acceptance decision (lesson 4.3).

> **Agents can read the whole course.** Every page has a Markdown version (see "For agents" in the page margin), and `/llms.txt` lists them all. Point an agent there when it needs context beyond a single exercise.

## In this chapter

- Leçon 1.1: [Ce que mesure un test de performance](/demo/fr/performance-testing/overview/what-it-measures.md) (20 min). Latence, débit et erreurs : les trois chiffres de tout test de performance, et pourquoi la latence s'exprime en percentiles.
- Leçon 1.2: [Tests statiques et dynamiques](/demo/fr/performance-testing/overview/static-and-dynamic.md) (20 min). Les deux familles de tests de performance, ce que chacune peut ou ne peut pas trouver, et comment préparer les questions avant de tester.
- Chapitre 1 · Résumé: [Vue d'ensemble : résumé](/demo/fr/performance-testing/overview/summary.md) (5 min). Le vocabulaire et le plan qui vous serviront pour la suite du cours.

# Leçon 1.1: Ce que mesure un test de performance

Tests de performance · Chapitre 1: Vue d'ensemble · 20 min

> Latence, débit et erreurs : les trois chiffres de tout test de performance, et pourquoi la latence s'exprime en percentiles.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

**Vous saurez:**
- Name the three numbers a performance test reports and what each says about users
- Read p50, p95 and p99, and explain why an average hides problems
- Run the practice app and take a first, repeatable measurement

## Transcription: What performance testing measures (1:31)

**0:00 Introduction.** Whatever tool you use, a performance test reports three numbers. Let's meet them.

**0:06 Three numbers.** Latency: how long one request takes, in milliseconds. Throughput: how many requests complete every second. And the error rate: the share of requests that fail or time out. They move together. As a system nears its limit, throughput stops rising, latency climbs, and soon after, errors appear.

**0:28 Percentiles.** Send the same request four hundred times and you get four hundred different durations. Stacked by duration, they form a hump, with a long tail of slow requests to the right. The median, or p50, is the typical request. Half are faster, half are slower. p95 and p99 describe the tail. One user in twenty waits at least as long as the p95. The average sits in between and describes no real request. That's why budgets and thresholds use percentiles.

**1:03 A first measurement.** In the exercise you'll start the practice app and ask it for one page of books. The response says it ran a hundred and one database queries. Then you'll put it under light load: ten virtual users for twenty seconds. On our machine that gave sixteen requests per second, with a p95 over a second. Write it down, with the command you ran. That's your baseline.

## La leçon

A performance test answers questions like "how long do customers wait?" and "how much traffic can we take before that gets worse?". Whatever the tool, the answers come back as three numbers.

| Number | Question it answers | Unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Latency** (response time) | How long does one request take? | milliseconds |
| **Throughput** | How many requests complete per second? | requests per second (req/s) |
| **Error rate** | What share of requests fail or time out? | percent |

They move together. When a system nears its limit, throughput stops rising, latency climbs, and soon after, errors appear. Chapter 3 shows that happening to Larkspur.

## Latency is a distribution

Send the same request a few hundred times and you get a few hundred different durations. Most are close together; a few are much slower, held up by a garbage-collection pause, a cold cache or a busy database. Play the animation to see the shape this makes.

> **Animation de concept: Latency is a distribution**
>
> 1. Every request takes a different amount of time. Here are 400 requests to the same endpoint.
> 2. Stacked by duration, they form a hump with a long tail to the right.
> 3. The median, p50, is the typical request: 95 ms. Half are faster, half are slower.
> 4. p95 and p99 describe the tail: 371 ms and 556 ms. One user in twenty waits at least 371 ms.
> 5. The average, 133 ms, describes no real request and hides the tail. Budgets and thresholds use percentiles.

Because of that long tail, latency is reported as **percentiles**. The p95 is the duration that 95% of requests beat; 5% are slower. Think of it as the experience of one user in twenty, which on a busy site is a lot of people.

| Statistic | What it tells you | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| p50 (median) | The typical request | Spotting broad regressions |
| p95 | The slow tail most users will eventually hit | Budgets and test thresholds |
| p99 | The worst regular experience | Systems where the tail matters (checkout, login) |
| max | One outlier | Investigating, never for budgets |
| average | Nothing a real user experienced | Avoid |

The average pulls toward the slow tail but still sits far below it, so it hides the requests people complain about. Every budget and threshold in this course uses percentiles.

## Throughput and errors

Throughput is the rate of completed requests. On its own it says little: 16 req/s is plenty for a small shop and a disaster for a ticket sale. It becomes useful next to latency, as in "16 req/s at p95 under 300 ms".

The error rate keeps the other two honest. A server that fails fast can post great latency numbers. Always check errors before you celebrate a speed-up.

## Measurements you can repeat

A number without its conditions is not a measurement. Record at least:

- the endpoint or page,
- how many virtual users, for how long,
- the machine and whether anything else was running,
- the exact command.

Then you, a teammate or an agent can run it again after a change and compare like with like.

## Hands-on: Set up Larkspur and take a first measurement

**Pratique · 15 min.** Objectif. Get the practice app running and record a baseline for /api/books: query count, p50, p95 and throughput at 10 users.

1. Build the database. It takes a few seconds and prints what it created.

   ```bash
   cd academy/practice/larkspur
   npm run seed
   ```

2. Start the app in its own terminal and leave it running.

   ```bash
   npm start
   # Larkspur Books on http://localhost:3000
   ```

![The Larkspur Books storefront: a header, a large photo of bookshelves with the heading 'Find your next favourite book', and a grid of new arrivals showing title, author, price and star rating.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (localhost:3000): The storefront you'll test. It loads slowly; chapter 3 explains why.*

3. Ask for one page of books and look at the headers. Larkspur reports how many database queries the request ran and how long the server spent on it.

   ```bash
   curl -s -i http://localhost:3000/api/books | head -4
   ```

   ```text
   HTTP/1.1 200 OK
   content-type: application/json
   x-query-count: 101
   server-timing: app;dur=60.4
   ```

   101 queries for one page of 50 books is worth remembering. Lesson 2.2 explains it.

4. Put it under light load: 10 virtual users for 20 seconds, using the load tool that ships with the app.

   ```bash
   npm run load -- --url http://localhost:3000/api/books --vus 10 --duration 20
   ```

![Terminal output of the mini load tool: one row for 10 virtual users over 20 seconds showing about 16 requests per second, p50 around 570 ms, p95 around 1,300 ms, 0 errors and 101 queries per request.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (npm run load): Your numbers will differ. On our machine: 16 req/s, p50 573 ms, p95 1,320 ms, 101 queries per request.*

5. Write the result to `notes/perf-baseline.md` with the command you ran. You'll compare against it after every fix.

**C'est terminé quand**
- notes/perf-baseline.md exists and every number in it appears in the command output you captured
- The baseline names the endpoint, the number of virtual users and the duration

**La part de l'agent : déléguez l'implémentation**

```text
You are doing a hands-on exercise from the "Performance Testing" course: Lesson 1.1, "What performance testing measures".

Exercise: Set up Larkspur and take a first measurement
Goal: Get the practice app running and record a baseline for /api/books: query count, p50, p95 and throughput at 10 users.

Project: academy/practice/larkspur (A Node.js 22 bookshop with a storefront and three JSON endpoints over SQLite. No dependencies. Slow on purpose.)
Setup, if not done already:
  cd academy/practice/larkspur
  npm run seed
  npm start   # leave it running in its own terminal; http://localhost:3000

Steps:
1. Run `npm run seed` and confirm it reports 500 authors, 5,000 books, 50,000 reviews and 200,000 orders.
2. Start the app with `npm start` in the background and wait until http://localhost:3000/health returns `ok`.
3. Run `curl -s -i http://localhost:3000/api/books` and note the `x-query-count` and `server-timing` headers.
4. Run `npm run load -- --url http://localhost:3000/api/books --vus 10 --duration 20` and capture the result row.
5. Create `notes/perf-baseline.md` inside the practice app with the date, the command used, and the measured requests/s, p50, p95, p99 and queries per request.
6. Stop the app when you're done.

Done when:
- notes/perf-baseline.md exists and every number in it appears in the command output you captured
- The baseline names the endpoint, the number of virtual users and the duration

Report back:
- The baseline table you wrote
- One sentence on what the query count suggests about the endpoint

Ground rules:
- Work inside academy/practice/larkspur. Don't add dependencies unless a step asks for one.
- Base every number you report on command output you actually ran. Quote it; don't estimate.
- If a step fails or a tool is missing, stop and report the exact error instead of working around it.

Lesson text, if you need more context: academy/src/content/lessons/en/performance-testing/1-overview/1-what-it-measures.mdx
```

## Points clés

- Latency is how long one request takes, throughput is how many complete per second, and the error rate is the share that fail.
- Latency is a distribution. Report percentiles: p50 for the typical request, p95 and p99 for the slow tail.
- An average blends fast and slow requests into a number no user experienced. Don't set budgets on averages.
- Write down how you measured (users, duration, endpoint), so the number can be repeated and compared.

# Leçon 1.2: Tests statiques et dynamiques

Tests de performance · Chapitre 1: Vue d'ensemble · 20 min

> Les deux familles de tests de performance, ce que chacune peut ou ne peut pas trouver, et comment préparer les questions avant de tester.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

**Vous saurez:**
- Explain the difference between static and dynamic performance testing
- Pick the cheaper test that can still answer a given question
- Write a short test plan: questions, budgets, risks and the tests that cover them

## Transcription: Static and dynamic testing (1:13)

**0:00 Introduction.** There are two ways to look for performance problems. You can read what you built, or you can run it and measure.

**0:09 Two families.** Static testing reads artifacts: code, query plans, build output and budgets. Nothing runs, so a static check takes seconds and can gate every pull request. It finds patterns that are known to be slow. Dynamic testing runs the system, and sends it traffic. It measures what users actually feel, finds problems nobody predicted, and proves that a fix worked.

**0:36 Side by side.** Side by side: static testing is cheap and early. Dynamic testing is slower, but it's the only way to see real impact. They work best together. Static checks catch common mistakes cheaply. Dynamic tests confirm the important ones, and find the rest.

**0:54 Start with questions.** Before you pick a tool, write down what you need to know. Good questions name a page or an endpoint, a load, and a number. Then pick the cheapest test that can answer each one. In the exercise, you'll write that plan for Larkspur.

## La leçon

There are two ways to look for performance problems. You can **read** what you built, or you can **run** it and measure. This course calls them static and dynamic testing, and spends a chapter on each.

> **Animation de concept: Two ways to test performance**
>
> 1. Static testing reads what you built: code, queries, assets and budgets.
> 2. Nothing runs, so it takes seconds and fits in every pull request. It finds likely problems.
> 3. Dynamic testing runs the system and sends it traffic.
> 4. It measures what users actually feel: response time, throughput and errors.

## Static testing

Static testing inspects artifacts: source code, SQL, build output, configuration, budgets. Nothing is deployed and no traffic is generated, so a static check runs in seconds and can gate every pull request.

It finds **patterns that are known to be slow**: a query inside a loop, a query plan that scans a whole table, a 600 KB script on the critical path. What it can't tell you is how much any of that hurts under real traffic, or find a problem that no rule describes.

## Dynamic testing

Dynamic testing runs the system and measures it: a lab page load with Lighthouse, a load test with k6, a CPU profile taken while traffic flows. It needs a running environment and minutes rather than seconds.

In exchange it reports what users would actually feel, finds problems nobody predicted, and proves that a fix worked.

| | Static | Dynamic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Looks at | Code, queries, assets, config | The running system |
| Speed | Seconds | Minutes to hours |
| Runs on | Every pull request | Staging, before a release, on a schedule |
| Finds | Known slow patterns | Real impact, unknown problems, capacity |
| Can't | Measure impact | Point to the line of code by itself |
| In this course | Chapter 2 | Chapter 3 |

The two work best together. Static checks catch the common mistakes cheaply; dynamic tests confirm the important ones and find the rest. Chapter 4 wires both into one workflow.

## Start a plan with questions

Before choosing a tool, write down what you need to know. Good questions name a page or endpoint, a load and a number:

- Can the storefront reach Largest Contentful Paint in under 2.5 s on a mid-range phone?
- Does `/api/books` keep p95 under 300 ms with 50 concurrent shoppers?
- How many users can the app serve before p95 passes the budget?
- Does the app stay stable over an hour of ordinary traffic?

Then pick the cheapest test that can answer each question, and note the risks you can already see in the code. That list is a test plan.

> **Test environments.** Dynamic results depend on the machine. Test on something close to production, or compare only runs from the same machine. A laptop is fine for learning and for before/after comparisons; it is not evidence of production capacity.

## Hands-on: Draft a performance test plan for Larkspur

**Pratique · 15 min.** Objectif. Write a one-page plan that lists the questions you'll answer about Larkspur, a budget for each, and whether a static or a dynamic test covers it.

1. Skim the app: `server.mjs`, the three files in `src/routes/`, `public/index.html` and `budget.json`. Don't run anything yet; this is a static read.
2. Create `notes/perf-plan.md` with four headings: **Questions**, **Budgets**, **Risks** and **Tests**.
3. Write at least four questions like the ones above, and give each a budget with a unit.
4. Under **Risks**, list what looks slow and where. Hint: look at what `listBooks` does inside its `for` loop.
5. Under **Tests**, say which tool answers each question. Use this table as a start:

   | Question or risk | Static check | Dynamic test |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | Page weight | `npm run budget` | Lighthouse |
   | Queries inside loops | `npm run lint:queries` | `x-query-count` under load |
   | Slow lookups | `npm run explain` | k6 load test |
   | Capacity | – | k6 stress test |

![A Markdown file open in an editor with four sections. Questions lists four items such as 'Does /api/books keep p95 under 300 ms with 50 users?'. Budgets gives numbers like 'p95 300 ms' and 'scripts 50 KB gzipped'. Risks cites src/routes/books.mjs line 11. Tests maps each item to a command.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (notes/perf-plan.md): A plan fits on one page. You'll fill in results as the course goes on.*

**C'est terminé quand**
- notes/perf-plan.md has the four sections
- Every budget is a number with a unit, and every question maps to at least one test
- Risks cite file paths and line numbers

**La part de l'agent : déléguez l'implémentation**

```text
You are doing a hands-on exercise from the "Performance Testing" course: Lesson 1.2, "Static and dynamic testing".

Exercise: Draft a performance test plan for Larkspur
Goal: Write a one-page plan that lists the questions you'll answer about Larkspur, a budget for each, and whether a static or a dynamic test covers it.

Project: academy/practice/larkspur (A Node.js 22 bookshop with a storefront and three JSON endpoints over SQLite. No dependencies. Slow on purpose.)
Setup, if not done already:
  cd academy/practice/larkspur
  npm run seed
  npm start   # leave it running in its own terminal; http://localhost:3000

Steps:
1. Read `README.md`, `server.mjs`, the files in `src/routes/`, `public/index.html` and `budget.json` to learn what the app does.
2. Create `notes/perf-plan.md` with four sections: Questions, Budgets, Risks, Tests.
3. Under Questions, list at least four concrete questions, each naming an endpoint or page and a number of users.
4. Under Budgets, give each question a measurable limit (for example p95 in ms, KB of assets, queries per request).
5. Under Risks, list anything in the code that looks likely to be slow, with file and line, without running the app.
6. Under Tests, map every question and risk to a static check or a dynamic test from this repository (`npm run budget`, `npm run lint:queries`, `npm run explain`, `npm run load`, the k6 scripts in `load/`).

Done when:
- notes/perf-plan.md has the four sections
- Every budget is a number with a unit, and every question maps to at least one test
- Risks cite file paths and line numbers

Report back:
- The Questions and Budgets sections
- The three risks you think are most serious, and why

Ground rules:
- Work inside academy/practice/larkspur. Don't add dependencies unless a step asks for one.
- Base every number you report on command output you actually ran. Quote it; don't estimate.
- If a step fails or a tool is missing, stop and report the exact error instead of working around it.

Lesson text, if you need more context: academy/src/content/lessons/en/performance-testing/1-overview/2-static-and-dynamic.mdx
```

## Points clés

- Static testing inspects code, queries, assets and configuration without running the system. It is fast and runs on every change, but it can only find likely problems.
- Dynamic testing runs the system under realistic traffic and measures what users feel. It is slower and needs an environment, but it proves the impact.
- Use static checks to catch known patterns early, and dynamic tests to confirm impact and find what no rule describes.
- Plan with questions first ("can checkout take 50 users at p95 under 300 ms?"), then choose the cheapest test that answers each one.

# Chapitre 1 · Résumé: Vue d'ensemble : résumé

Tests de performance · Chapitre 1: Vue d'ensemble · 5 min

> Le vocabulaire et le plan qui vous serviront pour la suite du cours.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

## Transcription: Overview: summary (0:36)

**0:00 Recap.** Here's what chapter one covered, in four points.

**0:04 Key points.** Every performance test reports latency, throughput and an error rate. Latency is a distribution, so we report percentiles, never the average. Static testing reads what you built. Dynamic testing runs it and measures. And a good plan starts with concrete questions, each with a number to hit.

**0:26 Next.** Next comes static testing: the cheapest tests there are. You'll find three of Larkspur's problems without starting the app at all.

## La leçon

You now have the vocabulary for the rest of the course, a running practice app, a baseline and a plan.

## Key points

### 1.1 Ce que mesure un test de performance

- Latency is how long one request takes, throughput is how many complete per second, and the error rate is the share that fail.
- Latency is a distribution. Report percentiles: p50 for the typical request, p95 and p99 for the slow tail.
- An average blends fast and slow requests into a number no user experienced. Don't set budgets on averages.
- Write down how you measured (users, duration, endpoint), so the number can be repeated and compared.

### 1.2 Tests statiques et dynamiques

- Static testing inspects code, queries, assets and configuration without running the system. It is fast and runs on every change, but it can only find likely problems.
- Dynamic testing runs the system under realistic traffic and measures what users feel. It is slower and needs an environment, but it proves the impact.
- Use static checks to catch known patterns early, and dynamic tests to confirm impact and find what no rule describes.
- Plan with questions first ("can checkout take 50 users at p95 under 300 ms?"), then choose the cheapest test that answers each one.

## Check yourself

1. A dashboard shows an average response time of 140 ms. Why isn't that enough to say the endpoint is fast?
   The average hides the tail. p95 could be several hundred milliseconds, meaning one user in twenty waits much longer. Ask for p95 and p99.
2. Which family of test would you use to check, on every pull request, that no one adds a 600 KB script to the storefront?
   A static check: measure the assets against a budget at build time. It takes seconds and needs no running server.
3. Your static checks all pass. Can you say the app handles 50 users at p95 under 300 ms?
   No. Static checks find known patterns; only a dynamic test under that load can show the p95 users would see.
4. What must you record next to a measured p95 so someone else can repeat it?
   The endpoint, the number of virtual users and the duration, the machine, and the exact command.

## Next

Chapter 2 starts with the cheapest tests there are: the ones that never run your code. You'll turn the budgets in your plan into a check that fails the build, then find three of Larkspur's problems by reading code, query plans and build output.

# Chapitre 2 · Ouverture: Tests statiques

Tests de performance · Chapitre 2: Tests statiques · 5 min

> Trouver les problèmes de performance en lisant ce que vous avez construit, avant toute exécution.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

## Transcription: Static testing (0:49)

**0:00 Introduction.** Chapter two is about the cheapest performance tests you will ever run: the ones that never start your code.

**0:08 What you'll get.** By the end of this chapter, you'll turn budgets into a check that fails the build, spot the N+1 query pattern, with a linter and by eye, read a query plan, and fix a full table scan with an index, and find what makes a page heavy, then cut it below budget.

**0:32 Your tools.** You'll use three tools that ship with the practice app. None of them needs a server. The trade-off: a static check finds what looks slow. It can't tell you how slow it is under load. That's chapter three's job.

## La leçon

Static tests are the cheapest performance tests you will ever run. They read code, query plans and build output, so they need no server, no traffic and no test environment. They take seconds, which means they can run on every change, long before anyone notices a slowdown.

The trade-off: a static check only finds problems that look like something already known to be slow. It tells you a query will scan 200,000 rows, not how many seconds that costs at 50 users. That's chapter 3's job. In this chapter you'll find three of Larkspur's problems without starting the app at all, then confirm each fix with one quick request.

## Ce que vous allez obtenir

- Turn your plan's budgets into a check that passes or fails the build
- Spot the N+1 query pattern in code, with a linter and by eye, and remove it
- Read a SQLite query plan, recognise a full table scan, and fix it with an index
- Find what makes a page heavy, and cut it below budget
- Know which of these checks belong on every pull request

## What you'll use

| Tool | What it reads | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `npm run budget` | The files the storefront loads, measured against `budget.json` | 2.1, 2.4 |
| `npm run lint:queries` | Source files, looking for database calls inside loops | 2.2 |
| `npm run explain` | SQLite's plan for a query, without running it | 2.3 |

All three ship with the practice app and need nothing installed.

## In this chapter

- Leçon 2.1: [Budgets de performance](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/budgets.md) (20 min). Se mettre d'accord sur des limites avant de mesurer, puis laisser un contrôle les faire respecter à chaque changement.
- Leçon 2.2: [Revue de code : les requêtes N+1](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/n-plus-one.md) (25 min). Le bug de performance le plus courant dans le code qui utilise une base de données, comment le trouver en lisant et comment l'éliminer.
- Leçon 2.3: [Lire les plans de requête](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/query-plans.md) (25 min). Demander à la base comment elle exécuterait une requête, sans l'exécuter, et corriger les parcours complets de table avec le bon index.
- Leçon 2.4: [Le poids des ressources](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/asset-weight.md) (20 min). Trouver ce qui alourdit une page en pesant ses fichiers, et la faire tenir dans le budget sans changer ce que voient les utilisateurs.
- Chapitre 2 · Résumé: [Tests statiques : résumé](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/summary.md) (5 min). Ce que vous avez trouvé sans exécuter l'application, et ce que les contrôles statiques ne peuvent pas vous dire.

Suivant: [Leçon 2.1: Budgets de performance](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/budgets.md)


# Leçon 2.1: Budgets de performance

Tests de performance · Chapitre 2: Tests statiques · 20 min

> Se mettre d'accord sur des limites avant de mesurer, puis laisser un contrôle les faire respecter à chaque changement.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

**Vous saurez:**
- Explain what a performance budget is and who should agree on it
- Choose budget metrics that can be checked statically and dynamically
- Run an asset budget check and read its result

## Transcription: Performance budgets (1:14)

**0:00 Introduction.** "Make it fast" isn't a requirement anyone can test. A performance budget is.

**0:06 How a budget works.** A budget is a limit the team agrees on before measuring. For Larkspur: fifty kilobytes of script, two hundred and fifty of images, three hundred and fifty in total. Then you measure the current build against each limit. Anything over its line fails. Larkspur is over on scripts, on images, and in total. A failed budget is a clear signal. With an exit code of one, it can block a pull request instead of starting a debate.

**0:39 Three kinds.** Budgets come in three kinds. Quantity budgets, like kilobytes or queries per request, can be checked statically, on every change. Timing budgets, like p95 or Largest Contentful Paint, need a dynamic test. Start from what users need, then from where you are today, and tighten the budget as you improve.

**1:01 Run the check.** In the exercise you'll run the budget check and see exactly which files push the page over. Two files account for almost all of it. Lesson 2.4 fixes them.

## La leçon

"Make it fast" isn't a requirement anyone can test. A **performance budget** is: a limit on a measurable quantity, agreed before anyone measures, that a check can enforce.

> **Animation de concept: A budget turns “fast enough” into pass or fail**
>
> 1. A budget is a limit the team agrees on before measuring: 50 KB of script, 250 KB of images, 350 KB in total.
> 2. Then measure the current build against each limit.
> 3. Anything over its line fails. Larkspur is over on scripts, images and total weight.
> 4. A failed budget is a clear signal. It can block a pull request instead of starting a debate.

## Three kinds of budget

| Kind | Examples | Checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Quantity** | JavaScript ≤ 50 KB gzipped, images ≤ 250 KB, ≤ 5 queries per request | Statically, on every build |
| **Timing** | p95 ≤ 300 ms at 50 users, LCP ≤ 2.5 s on a mid-range phone | Dynamically, with Lighthouse or k6 |
| **Rule-based** | Lighthouse performance score ≥ 90, no render-blocking scripts | Dynamically, with Lighthouse |

Quantity budgets are the static ones, and the most useful early on: they can't be argued with, and they catch regressions the moment someone commits them. A timing budget tells you whether users are happy; a quantity budget tells you which change made them unhappy.

## Where the numbers come from

Good budgets come from three places, in this order:

1. **What users need.** Google's Core Web Vitals call an LCP under 2.5 s "good". Studies of web shops put noticeable drop-off at around one second of extra delay.
2. **What competitors do.** If a rival's product page loads in 1.8 s, that's your bar.
3. **Where you are today.** A budget that fails on day one by a factor of ten will be switched off. Start at today's numbers, then ratchet down.

Larkspur's `budget.json` sets quantity limits for the storefront:

```json
{
  "page": "public/index.html",
  "budgets": { "script": 50, "stylesheet": 20, "image": 250, "total": 350 }
}
```

Scripts and stylesheets are measured gzipped, the way browsers download them; images as stored. The check script reads `index.html`, finds every script, stylesheet and image it references, weighs each file, and exits with code 1 if any budget is exceeded. Exit code 1 is what makes a CI job fail.

> **Budgets need an owner.** Agree budgets with whoever owns the product, not only the engineers. When a new feature needs more room, that's a product decision: raise the budget on purpose, or cut something else.

## Hands-on: Run the asset budget and record what fails

**Pratique · 10 min.** Objectif. Run Larkspur's asset budget, identify which files push it over, and add API timing budgets to your plan for chapter 3.

1. Run the check from the practice app folder. It doesn't need the app running.

   ```bash
   npm run budget
   ```

   ```text
   Asset weight for public/index.html

   type        size KB   file
   script         95.9   /vendor/datefmt-all-locales.js
   script          0.3   /app.js
   stylesheet      0.5   /styles.css
   image        1043.1   /hero.jpg

   budget      actual   limit   result
   script        96.2      50   FAIL  (+46.2 KB)
   stylesheet     0.5      20   pass
   image       1043.1     250   FAIL  (+793.1 KB)
   total       1139.8     350   FAIL  (+789.8 KB)

   3 budget(s) exceeded.
   ```

![Terminal showing the asset table and the budget table. Scripts 96.2 KB against 50, images 1043.1 KB against 250 and total 1139.8 KB against 350 are marked FAIL; stylesheets 0.5 KB pass.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (npm run budget): Three of four budgets fail. Two files account for almost all of it.*

2. Check the exit code. `echo $?` prints `1` right after a failed run, which is what stops a CI pipeline.
3. For each failure, name the file responsible. Here it's easy: one script and one image.
4. Add the API timing budgets from the agent prompt to `notes/perf-plan.md`. You'll turn them into k6 thresholds in lesson 3.2.

**C'est terminé quand**
- You have the budget output and its exit code
- Each failing budget is attributed to a specific file
- notes/perf-plan.md lists both asset and API budgets

## Points clés

- A budget is a limit agreed before measuring. It turns "is this fast enough?" into pass or fail.
- Quantity budgets (KB, requests, queries) can be checked statically on every change. Timing budgets (p95, LCP) need a dynamic test.
- Base budgets on user needs and competitors, then on today's numbers so they're achievable. Tighten them as you improve.
- A budget check that fails the build gets fixed. A dashboard that turns red gets ignored.

# Leçon 2.2: Revue de code : les requêtes N+1

Tests de performance · Chapitre 2: Tests statiques · 25 min

> Le bug de performance le plus courant dans le code qui utilise une base de données, comment le trouver en lisant et comment l'éliminer.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

**Vous saurez:**
- Recognise the N+1 query pattern in code
- Use a static check to flag database calls inside loops
- Rewrite an N+1 loop as a single query with joins, and verify the query count

## Transcription: Code review for N+1 queries (1:14)

**0:00 Introduction.** Here's the most common performance bug in database-backed code, and how to find it just by reading.

**0:07 Read the code.** This is the books endpoint. It fetches one page of fifty books in a single query. Then it loops over the books. Inside the loop, it asks the database for each book's author, and for each book's rating. That's two more queries for every book on the page.

**0:29 On a timeline.** On a timeline it looks like this. One query for the list, then a hundred small queries, one after another. A hundred and one round trips for one page. Each one is quick, but together they're most of the response time. One query with joins fetches exactly the same data in a single trip.

**0:53 Find it, fix it.** The pattern is easy to spot statically: a database call inside a loop. The practice app ships with a small linter that finds it. In the exercise you'll rewrite the loop as one query, and watch the query count drop from a hundred and one to one, with an identical response.

## La leçon

Here is the books endpoint that the storefront calls. Read it before reading on; the problem is visible.

```js title="src/routes/books.mjs"
export function listBooks(params) {
  const page = Math.max(1, Number(params.get("page")) || 1);
  const books = query(
    "SELECT id, title, author_id, price_cents FROM books ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET ?"
  ).all((page - 1) * 50);

  for (const book of books) {
    const author = query("SELECT name FROM authors WHERE id = ?").get(book.author_id);
    book.author = author.name;
    const rating = query("SELECT avg(stars) AS avg, count(*) AS n FROM reviews WHERE book_id = ?").get(book.id);
    book.rating = rating.avg ? Math.round(rating.avg * 10) / 10 : null;
    book.reviews = rating.n;
  }
  return { page, books };
}
```

## The N+1 pattern

One query fetches the list. Then the loop runs two more queries **for every item**. With 50 books that's 1 + 50 × 2 = 101 queries for one page.

> **Animation de concept: The N+1 query pattern**
>
> 1. The books endpoint asks the database for one page of 50 books. One query.
> 2. Then it loops over the books and asks for each one's author and rating: two more queries per book.
> 3. That's 101 round trips for one page. Each is small; together they're most of the response time.
> 4. One query with JOINs fetches the same data in a single trip.

Each query is cheap on its own, which is why N+1 survives code review and local testing: on a laptop with 10 rows, nobody notices. It grows with the page size and the data, and on a real network every query adds a round trip. ORMs make it easy to write by accident, because `book.author.name` can quietly run a query.

## Finding it statically

The shape is distinctive: a database call **inside a loop body**. That's easy to check without running anything. Larkspur includes a small linter that does exactly this:

```bash
npm run lint:queries
```

```text
src/routes/books.mjs:11  query inside a loop (possible N+1)
    const author = query("SELECT name FROM authors WHERE id = ?").get(book.author_id);
src/routes/books.mjs:13  query inside a loop (possible N+1)
    const rating = query("SELECT avg(stars) AS avg, count(*) AS n FROM reviews WHERE book_id = ?").get(book.id);

2 possible N+1 pattern(s).
```

It's a heuristic. It reads source text and tracks loop bodies, so it can miss a query hidden behind a helper function and can flag a loop that only ever runs once. Treat each finding as a question for code review. Real projects use the same idea at a larger scale: ORM-specific lint rules, or a test that fails if an endpoint runs more than N queries.

## Fixing it

Ask the database for everything in one go. SQL is built for this: join the authors, aggregate the reviews, and group by book.

```js title="src/routes/books.mjs (after)"
export function listBooks(params) {
  const page = Math.max(1, Number(params.get("page")) || 1);
  const books = query(`
    SELECT b.id, b.title, b.author_id, b.price_cents, a.name AS author,
           round(avg(r.stars), 1) AS rating, count(r.id) AS reviews
    FROM (SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET ?) AS b
    JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
    LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.book_id = b.id
    GROUP BY b.id
    ORDER BY b.id`).all((page - 1) * 50);
  return { page, books };
}
```

When a join isn't practical (the data lives in another service, say), **batch** instead: collect the IDs and fetch them in one `WHERE id IN (...)` query. Either way the query count stops depending on the page size.

| | Queries per request | Server time, one request |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before | 101 | 60 ms |
| After the join | 1 | 26 ms |

Better, but 26 ms for 50 rows is still slow. The join reads the reviews table in a way that needs an index. That's lesson 2.3.

## Hands-on: Find and remove the N+1 in /api/books

**Pratique · 20 min.** Objectif. Use the query linter to find the N+1 in the books endpoint, rewrite it as one query, and show the query count drop from 101 to 1 with the same response.

1. Run `npm run lint:queries`. You should get the two findings above.
2. Start the app and save the current response, so you can prove the fix changes nothing visible:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/books > /tmp/books-before.json
   curl -s -i http://localhost:3000/api/books | grep -i -E "x-query-count|server-timing"
   ```

3. Replace `listBooks` with the single-query version, restart the app, and fetch again into `/tmp/books-after.json`.
4. Compare the two files. They should be identical:

   ```bash
   node -e 'const a=require("/tmp/books-before.json"),b=require("/tmp/books-after.json");console.log(JSON.stringify(a)===JSON.stringify(b)?"identical":"DIFFERENT")'
   ```

![Terminal showing x-query-count: 1 and server-timing around 26 ms for /api/books, the word 'identical' from the comparison, and 'No queries inside loops found.' from the linter.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (curl and lint:queries): One query, same response, linter clean.*

5. Run `npm run lint:queries` again. It should report nothing and exit 0.

**C'est terminé quand**
- `npm run lint:queries` reports no queries inside loops and exits 0
- `x-query-count` for /api/books is 1
- The before and after JSON responses are identical

**La part de l'agent : déléguez l'implémentation**

```text

Goal: Use the query linter to find the N+1 in the books endpoint, rewrite it as one query, and show the query count drop from 101 to 1 with the same response.

Project: academy/practice/larkspur (A Node.js 22 bookshop with a storefront and three JSON endpoints over SQLite. No dependencies. Slow on purpose.)

  cd academy/practice/larkspur

Keep the response shape: page, books[] with id, title, author_id, price_cents, author, rating, reviews.

- If a step fails or a tool is missing, stop and report the exact error instead of working around it.

Lesson text, if you need more context: academy/src/content/lessons/en/performance-testing/2-static/2-n-plus-one.mdx
```

## Points clés

- N+1 means one query for a list, then one more per item. The cost grows with the list and hides in fast local databases.
- Statically, it looks like a database call inside a loop or a .map callback. A simple lint rule catches most cases.
- Fix it by fetching everything in one query (JOIN, GROUP BY) or in one batched query (WHERE id IN (...)).
- Count queries per request. A count that grows with the page size is the signature of N+1.

# Leçon 2.3: Lire les plans de requête

Tests de performance · Chapitre 2: Tests statiques · 25 min

> Demander à la base comment elle exécuterait une requête, sans l'exécuter, et corriger les parcours complets de table avec le bon index.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

**Vous saurez:**
- Get a query plan from SQLite with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
- Tell a SCAN from a SEARCH, and know when a scan is a problem
- Design an index for a query's WHERE and ORDER BY, add it as a migration, and confirm the plan changed

## Transcription: Reading query plans (1:17)

**0:00 Introduction.** A query says what you want. The database decides how to get it. That decision is the query plan, and you can read it without running the query.

**0:12 Ask for the plan.** Here's the plan for one customer's twenty latest orders. Two warnings. SCAN orders means reading all two hundred thousand rows. And a temporary B-tree means sorting the matches afterwards.

**0:25 SCAN versus SEARCH.** Without an index, SQLite has to read every row of the orders table to find one customer's handful. That's what SCAN means, and it gets slower every day the table grows. An index keeps the emails sorted, like the index at the back of a book. SQLite walks down a few levels to the right entry. SEARCH using an index: a handful of page reads instead of two hundred thousand rows.

**0:56 Add the index.** Index the column you filter on first, then the column you sort by. Add it as a migration. Explain again. The scan has become a search, and the sort step is gone. On our machine, the orders endpoint went from eleven milliseconds to a tenth of a millisecond.

## La leçon

A query says **what** you want. The database decides **how** to get it: which table to read first, whether to use an index, whether to sort. That decision is the **query plan**, and every serious database will show it to you without running the query. Reading plans is static testing for SQL.

## SCAN versus SEARCH

The orders endpoint asks for one customer's 20 latest orders:

```sql
SELECT id, book_id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_email = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
```

Ask SQLite how it would run that:

```bash
npm run explain -- "SELECT id, book_id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_email = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20"
```

```text
QUERY PLAN
└─ SCAN orders   ← full table scan (200,000 rows)
└─ USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
```

Two warnings in two lines. `SCAN orders` means SQLite will read every one of the 200,000 rows to find one customer's 13. `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` means it will then sort the matches in a temporary structure.

> **Animation de concept: SCAN versus SEARCH**
>
> 1. To find one customer's orders without an index, SQLite has to read every row of the orders table: 200,000 of them.
> 2. That's what SCAN orders means in a query plan. It gets slower as the table grows.
> 3. An index keeps the emails sorted, like the index at the back of a book. SQLite walks down a few levels to the right entry.
> 4. SEARCH orders USING INDEX: a handful of page reads instead of 200,000 rows, and it barely grows with the table.

`SCAN` isn't always bad. In the books query from lesson 2.2, `SCAN books` sits inside a `LIMIT 50` subquery, so it stops after 50 rows. And scanning a 30-row lookup table is faster than any index. The question to ask is: **how many rows will this read, and how often does it run?** A full scan of a large table on a request path is a bug that gets worse every day the table grows.

## Designing the index

An index is a sorted copy of some columns, with a pointer back to each row. Pick its columns in this order:

1. **Columns you filter on with `=`**: here, `customer_email`.
2. **Columns you sort by**: here, `created_at`. Because the index is already sorted by email and then date, SQLite can read the newest 20 straight off it and skip the sort.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_email ON orders(customer_email, created_at);
```

The reviews lookup from lesson 2.2 has the same problem: `WHERE book_id = ?` with no index on `book_id` means scanning 50,000 reviews. After the join fix it happens once per page instead of 50 times, but it's still a scan.

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_reviews_book ON reviews(book_id);
```

> **Indexes aren't free.** Every index makes inserts and updates a little slower and takes disk space. Add indexes for queries that run often or on large tables, check the plan uses them, and drop the ones nothing uses.

## Hands-on: Turn two full table scans into index searches

**Pratique · 20 min.** Objectif. Find the full table scans behind /api/orders and the books page, add indexes in a migration, and confirm both plans and timings improve.

1. Run both `explain` commands from the agent prompt and keep the output. Both should end in `full table scan`.
2. With the app running, measure before you change anything:

   ```bash
   for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -s -o /dev/null -D - "http://localhost:3000/api/orders?email=reader42@larkspur.test" | grep -i server-timing; done
   ```

3. Create the migration. Migrations are SQL files in `db/migrations/`, applied in name order and recorded so they only run once:

   ```sql title="db/migrations/001_indexes.sql"
   CREATE INDEX idx_orders_email ON orders(customer_email, created_at);
   CREATE INDEX idx_reviews_book ON reviews(book_id);
   ```

   ```bash
   npm run migrate
   # applied 001_indexes.sql (140 ms)
   ```

4. Explain both queries again.

   ```text
   QUERY PLAN
   └─ SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_email (customer_email=?)
   ```

   The sort step is gone too: the index already delivers rows in date order.

![Two query plans one above the other. The first, before the migration, reads 'SCAN orders ← full table scan (200,000 rows)' and 'USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY'. The second, after, reads 'SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_email (customer_email=?)'.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (npm run explain): Before and after the migration: a scan of 200,000 rows becomes an index search.*

5. Restart the app and measure again. On our machine:

   | Endpoint | Before | After |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | `/api/orders` | 11 ms | 0.1 ms |
   | `/api/books` (with the join from 2.2) | 26 ms | 0.5 ms |

**C'est terminé quand**
- Neither plan contains 'full table scan'
- Both plans show SEARCH ... USING INDEX
- `npm run migrate` reports the migration applied, and running it again reports nothing to migrate

**La part de l'agent : déléguez l'implémentation**

```text
You are doing a hands-on exercise from the "Performance Testing" course: Lesson 2.3, "Reading query plans".

Exercise: Turn two full table scans into index searches
Goal: Find the full table scans behind /api/orders and the books page, add indexes in a migration, and confirm both plans and timings improve.

Project: academy/practice/larkspur (A Node.js 22 bookshop with a storefront and three JSON endpoints over SQLite. No dependencies. Slow on purpose.)
Setup, if not done already:
  cd academy/practice/larkspur
  npm run seed
  npm start   # leave it running in its own terminal; http://localhost:3000

Steps:
1. Run `npm run explain -- "SELECT id, book_id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_email = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20"` and capture the plan.
2. Run `npm run explain -- "SELECT avg(stars) FROM reviews WHERE book_id = ?"` and capture the plan.
3. Create `db/migrations/001_indexes.sql` with `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_email ON orders(customer_email, created_at);` and `CREATE INDEX idx_reviews_book ON reviews(book_id);`.
4. Run `npm run migrate`.
5. Run both explain commands again and capture the new plans.
6. With the app running, compare the `server-timing` header of /api/orders?email=reader42@larkspur.test and /api/books before and after (restart the app after migrating; take the median of five requests each).

Done when:
- Neither plan contains 'full table scan'
- Both plans show SEARCH ... USING INDEX
- `npm run migrate` reports the migration applied, and running it again reports nothing to migrate

Report back:
- Both plans before and after
- server-timing medians before and after for both endpoints

Ground rules:
- Work inside academy/practice/larkspur. Don't add dependencies unless a step asks for one.
- Base every number you report on command output you actually ran. Quote it; don't estimate.
- If a step fails or a tool is missing, stop and report the exact error instead of working around it.

Lesson text, if you need more context: academy/src/content/lessons/en/performance-testing/2-static/3-query-plans.mdx
```

## Points clés

- EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows how the database will run a query, without running it. That makes it a static check.
- SCAN reads every row of a table; SEARCH uses an index to jump to the matching rows. A SCAN of a large table on a hot path is a bug.
- Index the columns you filter on first, then the columns you sort by, so the database can skip the sort too.
- Indexes speed up reads and slow down writes. Add the ones your queries need, not one per column.

---

Suivant: [Leçon 2.4: Le poids des ressources](/demo/fr/performance-testing/static/asset-weight.md)


# Leçon 2.4: Le poids des ressources

Tests de performance · Chapitre 2: Tests statiques · 20 min

> Trouver ce qui alourdit une page en pesant ses fichiers, et la faire tenir dans le budget sans changer ce que voient les utilisateurs.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

**Vous saurez:**
- Find the heaviest files a page loads and judge whether they're needed
- Recognise render-blocking scripts in a page's HTML
- Cut page weight below budget and prove it with the budget check

## Transcription: Asset weight (1:15)

**0:00 Introduction.** The budget check said the storefront is over. Now let's find out exactly what makes it heavy.

**0:07 Where the weight goes.** Here's every file the storefront loads, drawn to scale. One thousand one hundred and forty kilobytes, against a budget of three hundred and fifty. Two files are nearly all of it: a hero photo saved at camera size, and a date library that bundles four hundred and twenty locales, when the shop uses one. Swap in the twelve-hundred-pixel export of the photo, and the English-only build of the library. From one thousand one hundred and forty kilobytes to fifty-nine. The customer sees the same page.

**0:44 Render-blocking scripts.** There's a second problem in the HTML. A plain script tag in the head stops the page from rendering until the script has downloaded and run. Add defer, and use the English-only file. The browser renders first, and runs the scripts afterwards, in order. Then point the image at the smaller export, with its width and height.

**1:08 Check again.** Run the budget again. Fifty-nine kilobytes, every budget met, and nothing changed for the customer.

## La leçon

Lesson 2.1's budget check found the storefront at 1,140 KB against a 350 KB budget. A budget failure tells you **that** something is too big. Weighing the files tells you **what**.

> **Animation de concept: Where the page weight goes**
>
> 1. Every file the storefront loads, drawn to scale by size. 1,140 KB against a 350 KB budget.
> 2. Two files are nearly all of it: a hero photo saved at 2400 pixels and quality 97, and a date library bundling 420 locales when the shop uses one.
> 3. Swap in the 1200-pixel export and the English-only locale file.
> 4. From 1,140 KB to 59 KB. The customer sees the same page.

## Ask two questions of every heavy file

**Is all of it needed?** `datefmt-all-locales.js` formats dates in 420 locales. The page calls it once, in `en-US`. The same library ships a single-locale build, `datefmt-en.js`, at 1.5 KB instead of 600 KB. This is the most common weight problem on the web: a whole library, or every locale, icon or polyfill, shipped for one use.

**Is it the right size?** `hero.jpg` is 2400 × 1200 pixels at JPEG quality 97, saved straight from a camera or design tool. The page displays it at most 1200 pixels wide. An export at the display size and quality 72, `hero-1200.jpg`, is 58 KB instead of 1 MB, and looks the same on screen.

## Render-blocking scripts

Weight isn't the only static warning in the HTML. Look at the head:

```html
<script src="/vendor/datefmt-all-locales.js"></script>
<script src="/app.js"></script>
```

A plain `<script>` tag in `<head>` stops the browser from rendering anything until the script has downloaded and run. With a 600 KB script on a phone connection, that's seconds of blank screen. Chapter 3 measures exactly how many.

Add `defer` and the browser downloads the scripts in parallel, renders the page, then runs them in order. `app.js` already waits for `DOMContentLoaded`, so nothing else has to change.

```html
<script src="/vendor/datefmt-en.js" defer></script>
<script src="/app.js" defer></script>
```

> **Width and height on images.** Give images `width` and `height` attributes. The browser can then reserve the space before the image arrives, so the text below it doesn't jump (that jump is measured as Cumulative Layout Shift). `fetchpriority="high"` on the main image tells the browser to fetch it early.

## Hands-on: Bring the storefront under budget

**Pratique · 15 min.** Objectif. Fix the two heaviest assets and the render-blocking scripts in public/index.html until npm run budget passes, without changing what the page shows.

1. Edit `public/index.html`. Leave `public/before.html` alone; it's a frozen copy for comparisons in chapter 3.

   ```diff
   - <script src="/vendor/datefmt-all-locales.js"></script>
   - <script src="/app.js"></script>
   + <script src="/vendor/datefmt-en.js" defer></script>
   + <script src="/app.js" defer></script>
   ...
   - <img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Shelves of books in warm light">
   + <img src="/hero-1200.jpg" width="1200" height="600" fetchpriority="high" alt="Shelves of books in warm light">
   ```

2. Run the budget check again.

   ```text
   budget      actual   limit   result
   script         0.9      50   pass
   stylesheet     0.5      20   pass
   image         57.6     250   pass
   total         59.0     350   pass

   All budgets met.
   ```

![Terminal showing the budget table after the fix: script 0.9 KB, stylesheet 0.5 KB, image 57.6 KB and total 59.0 KB, all marked pass, followed by 'All budgets met.'](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (npm run budget): From 1,140 KB to 59 KB.*

3. Open the storefront and check nothing changed for the customer: the photo, the "Updated" date line and the book grid should all be there.

![The Larkspur storefront after the fix. It looks the same as before: the bookshelf photo with the heading, an 'Updated' line with today's date, and the grid of new arrivals.](screenshot-pending)
*Screenshot (localhost:3000): Same page, a twentieth of the weight.*

**C'est terminé quand**
- `npm run budget` passes all budgets and exits 0
- public/before.html is unchanged
- The page still shows the updated date and the book grid

**La part de l'agent : déléguez l'implémentation**

```text
You are doing a hands-on exercise from the "Performance Testing" course: Lesson 2.4, "Asset weight".

Exercise: Bring the storefront under budget
Goal: Fix the two heaviest assets and the render-blocking scripts in public/index.html until npm run budget passes, without changing what the page shows.

Project: academy/practice/larkspur (A Node.js 22 bookshop with a storefront and three JSON endpoints over SQLite. No dependencies. Slow on purpose.)
Setup, if not done already:
  cd academy/practice/larkspur
  npm run seed
  npm start   # leave it running in its own terminal; http://localhost:3000

Steps:
1. Run `npm run budget` and note the failing budgets.
2. In `public/index.html` only (leave `public/before.html` untouched), replace `/vendor/datefmt-all-locales.js` with `/vendor/datefmt-en.js`; the page only formats dates in en-US.
3. Add `defer` to both script tags so they no longer block rendering. `app.js` already waits for DOMContentLoaded, and deferred scripts run in order.
4. Replace `/hero.jpg` with `/hero-1200.jpg` and add `width="1200" height="600"` and `fetchpriority="high"` to the img tag.
5. Run `npm run budget` again.
6. Start the app and load http://localhost:3000/ in a browser or with Playwright if available, and confirm the 'Updated <date>' line and the book grid still render. If no browser is available, say so.

Done when:
- `npm run budget` passes all budgets and exits 0
- public/before.html is unchanged
- The page still shows the updated date and the book grid

Report back:
- The budget output before and after
- The diff of public/index.html
- How you confirmed the page still renders correctly

Ground rules:
- Work inside academy/practice/larkspur. Don't add dependencies unless a step asks for one.
- Base every number you report on command output you actually ran. Quote it; don't estimate.
- If a step fails or a tool is missing, stop and report the exact error instead of working around it.

Lesson text, if you need more context: academy/src/content/lessons/en/performance-testing/2-static/4-asset-weight.mdx
```

## Points clés

- Weigh what the page actually loads. A few files are usually most of the weight.
- Ask of each heavy file: is all of it needed, and is it needed now? Libraries often bundle far more than you use.
- A plain <script> in <head> blocks rendering until it downloads and runs. Use defer, or move it.
- Serve images at the size they're displayed, compressed sensibly, and give them width and height.

# Chapitre 2 · Résumé: Tests statiques : résumé

Tests de performance · Chapitre 2: Tests statiques · 5 min

> Ce que vous avez trouvé sans exécuter l'application, et ce que les contrôles statiques ne peuvent pas vous dire.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

## Transcription: Static testing: summary (0:41)

**0:00 Recap.** Without generating any traffic, you found and fixed three problems.

**0:05 Results.** A hundred and one queries per page became one. Two full table scans became index searches. And the storefront went from over a megabyte to fifty-nine kilobytes. Each check took seconds.

**0:19 The limits.** But every fix came from a known pattern. None of these checks told you how the app behaves with fifty shoppers, how long a phone shows a blank screen, or what the processor is doing. And one endpoint, recommendations, didn't trigger a single warning. It's slow anyway. That's chapter three.

## La leçon

Without generating any traffic, you found and fixed three problems: 101 queries per page, two full table scans, and a page twenty times heavier than it needed to be. Each check takes seconds, and each would have caught its problem in the pull request that introduced it.

## Key points

### 2.1 Budgets de performance

- A budget is a limit agreed before measuring. It turns "is this fast enough?" into pass or fail.
- Quantity budgets (KB, requests, queries) can be checked statically on every change. Timing budgets (p95, LCP) need a dynamic test.
- Base budgets on user needs and competitors, then on today's numbers so they're achievable. Tighten them as you improve.
- A budget check that fails the build gets fixed. A dashboard that turns red gets ignored.

### 2.2 Revue de code : les requêtes N+1

- N+1 means one query for a list, then one more per item. The cost grows with the list and hides in fast local databases.
- Statically, it looks like a database call inside a loop or a .map callback. A simple lint rule catches most cases.
- Fix it by fetching everything in one query (JOIN, GROUP BY) or in one batched query (WHERE id IN (...)).
- Count queries per request. A count that grows with the page size is the signature of N+1.

### 2.3 Lire les plans de requête

- EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows how the database will run a query, without running it. That makes it a static check.
- SCAN reads every row of a table; SEARCH uses an index to jump to the matching rows. A SCAN of a large table on a hot path is a bug.
- Index the columns you filter on first, then the columns you sort by, so the database can skip the sort too.
- Indexes speed up reads and slow down writes. Add the ones your queries need, not one per column.

### 2.4 Le poids des ressources

- Weigh what the page actually loads. A few files are usually most of the weight.
- Ask of each heavy file: is all of it needed, and is it needed now? Libraries often bundle far more than you use.
- A plain <script> in <head> blocks rendering until it downloads and runs. Use defer, or move it.
- Serve images at the size they're displayed, compressed sensibly, and give them width and height.

## What static testing didn't tell you

Every fix in this chapter was guided by a pattern: a loop with a query, a scan in a plan, a heavy file. None of them told you how the app behaves when 50 people shop at once, how long the page takes to appear on a phone, or what happens to the CPU. And `/api/recommendations` didn't trigger a single static warning. It's slow anyway, as chapter 3 will show.

## Check yourself

1. A pull request adds a 40 KB charting library to every page. Which check from this chapter fails, and why is that the right place to catch it?
   The asset budget (script, 50 KB). It runs in seconds on the pull request, before the change ships, and names the file responsible.
2. The query linter reports no findings. Does that prove the code has no N+1 queries?
   No. It's a heuristic that reads loops in source text. A query behind a helper function, or an ORM loading relations lazily, can still cause N+1. Watch the query count per request too.
3. A plan shows SCAN countries (240 rows). Should you add an index?
   Probably not. Scanning 240 rows is cheap and the table won't grow much. Scans matter on large or growing tables on hot paths.
4. Why do these static checks still leave you unable to promise p95 under 300 ms at 50 users?
   They find known slow patterns but don't measure time under load. Only a dynamic test can show the latency users would see.

---

Suivant: [Chapitre 3 · Ouverture: Tests dynamiques](/demo/fr/performance-testing/dynamic.md)


# Chapitre 3 · Ouverture: Tests dynamiques

Tests de performance · Chapitre 3: Tests dynamiques · 5 min

> Faire tourner le système, lui envoyer du trafic et mesurer ce que ressentent vraiment les utilisateurs.

*Cette leçon n'est pas encore traduite en fr : vous lisez le texte anglais. Le titre et la navigation sont traduits.*

## Transcription: Dynamic testing (1:01)

**0:00 Introduction.** Chapter two found problems by reading. Chapter three finds them by running: loading the page the way a phone would, and sending the app the traffic of a busy evening.

**0:12 What you'll get.** You'll measure page load in the lab with Lighthouse, and read what the numbers mean for a phone. You'll write a load test with k6, and let thresholds decide whether the app meets its budgets. You'll push past the expected load to find the app's capacity, and check it survives a surge. And you'll profile the app under load, read a flame graph, and prove a fix with numbers.

**0:43 Before you start.** You'll need k6, a free load testing tool. If you can't install it, every exercise also works with the practice app's built-in load tool. And run tests from a quiet machine. Numbers from a busy laptop, or from two different machines, aren't comparable.

## La leçon

Chapter 2 found problems by reading. This chapter finds them by running: loading the page the way a phone would, sending the app the traffic of a busy evening, then more traffic until it bends, and finally looking inside the process while it struggles.

Dynamic tests cost more than static ones. They need the app running, they take minutes, and their numbers depend on the machine. In return they answer the questions static checks can't: how slow, for how many users, and why.

## Ce que vous allez obtenir

- Measure page load in the lab with Lighthouse and read FCP, LCP and the score
- Write a k6 load test with stages, checks and thresholds, and read its summary
- Run stress, spike and soak tests, and find the app's practical capacity
- Profile the app under load, read a flame graph, and prove a CPU fix with numbers

## Before you start

Install k6, the load testing tool this chapter uses:

| System | Command |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | `brew install k6` |
| Windows | `winget install k6 --source winget` |
| Debian, Ubuntu | see [grafana.com/docs/k6](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/set-up/install-k6/) |

If you can't install it, every exercise also works with the practice app's built-in tool, `npm run load`. You'll need Chrome for Lighthouse and the profiler.

> **Run tests from a quiet machine.** Close heavy apps before a dynamic test and run the load generator and the app on the same machine only when comparing before with after. Numbers from different machines, or from a busy laptop, aren't comparable.

## In this chapter

- Leçon 3.1: [Mesure en laboratoire avec Lighthouse](/demo/fr/performance-testing/dynamic/lighthouse.md) (25 min). Charger la page sur un téléphone simulé et mesurer ce que voit l'utilisateur, et à quel moment.
- Leçon 3.2: [Tests de charge avec k6](/demo/fr/performance-testing/dynamic/load-testing.md) (30 min). Simuler une soirée chargée d'acheteurs et laisser les seuils décider si l'application respecte ses budgets.
- Leçon 3.3: [Tests de stress, de pic et d'endurance](/demo/fr/performance-testing/dynamic/stress-spike-soak.md) (30 min). Dépasser la charge attendue pour trouver le plafond, survivre à un afflux et repérer les dérives lentes sur plusieurs heures.
- Leçon 3.4: [Trouver le goulot d'étranglement](/demo/fr/performance-testing/dynamic/bottlenecks.md) (30 min). Profiler l'application sous charge, lire le flame graph, corriger le chemin critique et le prouver avec le même test.
- Chapitre 3 · Résumé: [Tests dynamiques : résumé](/demo/fr/performance-testing/dynamic/summary.md) (5 min). Ce que l'exécution de l'application vous a appris et que la lecture ne pouvait pas révéler.
